newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam, U.S. reach "historic" copyright agreement.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam, U.S. reach "historic" copyright agreement.

text.p: The United States and Vietnam have agreed on a bilateral treaty which will provide legal protection for U.S. copyright owners in a country riddled with piracy, the U.S. Information Service in Hanoi said on Thursday.
Vietnamese authors and producers will have similar protection in the United States.
The deal, hammered out after three days of negotiations, takes the two former foes a step closer to their so-far elusive goal of normalising economic relations.

"This historic agreement creates, for the first time, a legal framework to protect the artistic, musical, literary, cinematic, choreographic, computer software and other works of both countries from copyright infringement," the USIS said in a statement.
It said the agreement would be signed shortly, after both sides have approved authoritative Vietnamese and English texts, and would go into effect not more than six months after signing.
The International Intellectual Property Alliance (IIPA), a coalition of associations representing U.S. copyright-based industries, issued a statement welcoming the agreement.
It said the treaty meant Vietnam would have to bring its copyright laws and enforcement practices closer to world standards and treat U.S. and local copyright owners equally.
Piracy of movies, videos. musical recordings, books, software and video games is rife in Vietnam, one of the poorest countries in the world.

High-quality copies of foreign compact discs sell in music stores for around $2 each and the U.S. computer giant Microsoft Corp said last December that an estimated 99 percent of software in Vietnam was pirated.
IIPA said piracy of copyright materials was inflicting over $50 million in trade losses anually and threatening the potential for U.S. exports to one of the world's fastest growing markets.
"This piracy problem must be tackled immediately if U.S.-Vietnam trade relations are ever to grow," it said. "The signing of this treaty could be just the breakthrough that is needed."

Hanoi and Washington normalised diplomatic ties in 1995, but progress towards a full trade agreement -- which would lead to most-favoured nation (MFN) trading status for Vietnam -- has so far been slow.
Joseph Damond, chief negotiator from the U.S. trade mission in Hanoi, said the copyright deal was "a good start" in that process, but gave no date for likely full economic normalisation.
